title: Hippocampal sleep replay distills old KV cache into memory tokens
idea: During idle accelerator slots (the analog of slow-wave sleep), a small consolidation network replays each long session's KV cache and distills spans of 64-256 tokens into 4-8 learned 'memory tokens' that reproduce their attention contribution; the originals are freed. Recent tokens stay verbatim (hippocampus) while old context lives as consolidated gist (neocortex).
why: Capacity: long-context KV is the largest inference DRAM consumer; claims 10-30x reduction on context older than a few thousand tokens.

title: Synaptic tag-and-capture promotes only reinforced KV entries
idea: New KV entries are written provisionally at 2-4 bit into a small scratch ring carrying a decaying 'tag'; only entries that receive above-threshold attention mass while tagged 'capture' promotion to full-precision storage, mirroring synaptic tagging and capture in long-term potentiation. Untagged entries expire or remain as 2-bit sketches.
why: KV capacity: most tokens never receive meaningful attention; 3-6x KV footprint reduction with bounded accuracy loss.

title: Clonal-selection antibody codebook compresses frequent cache-line patterns
idea: The memory controller keeps a 4K-entry 'antibody repertoire' of 64-byte line patterns; a line matching an antibody within a few bit flips is stored as a 12-bit pointer plus a sparse mutation mask. Antibodies that match often are cloned and hypermutated into variants and unused ones die, so the codebook evolves per workload like adaptive immunity.
why: Effective capacity: adaptive line-level compression, 1.5-3x on weights, page tables and zero-heavy activations, no software changes.

title: Epigenetic methylation bits trigger heterochromatin-style in-place page compaction
idea: Each 4 KB page carries 2 'methylation' bits set by the OS or ML runtime; methylated pages are packed by the controller into dense heterochromatin form (entropy-coded, 3-4x) inside the same DIMM while acetylated pages stay open and uncompressed. Marks are inherited by forked or copied pages, like epigenetic inheritance through cell division.
why: Capacity: software-hinted compression tier without a separate far-memory device; 30-50% fewer DRAM bits per server.

title: Physarum tube-reinforcement solver places pages across pooled CXL memory
idea: Each host-to-memory-node path is modeled as a slime-mould tube whose conductance grows with page traffic and decays otherwise; pages migrate along thickening tubes, so the pool converges on a minimal network where a shared page lives once, near its heaviest consumers, instead of being replicated per host.
why: Stranded and replicated DRAM in racks: 20-35% less total DRAM at near-local latency.

title: Pheromone-trail hash marks let tenants converge on shared pages
idea: A CXL switch keeps a decaying 'pheromone' table of content hashes recently written by any VM; when another tenant writes a page whose hash hits a strong trail, the switch maps it copy-on-write to the existing physical page. Trails evaporate, so only popular content (OS images, model weights, libraries) is deduplicated, without full memory scans.
why: Multi-tenant capacity: 15-40% dedup across VMs and inference replicas at negligible scan cost.

title: Foveated KV precision falls off with attention eccentricity
idea: Like the retina's dense fovea and sparse periphery, each attention head stores KV at 8-bit for the top-attended 5% of tokens, 4-bit for the next band and 1-2-bit sketches for the periphery; a 'saccade' (attention shift onto a peripheral token) re-fetches its full-precision copy from a compressed backing tier.
why: KV capacity and bandwidth: 3-5x fewer bits per token at near-baseline quality.

title: Developmental genome grows weights from seeds and growth rules
idea: Each weight matrix is stored as a compact 'genome' (PRNG seeds, a small hypernetwork and low-rank corrections) that is expanded tile-by-tile into SRAM at use time, the way a genome encodes a body plan instead of every cell's coordinates; DRAM holds only the genome.
why: Weight capacity: 10-50x smaller resident footprint for layers that tolerate generative parameterization, trading cheap compute for scarce DRAM bits.

title: Octopus-arm memory modules reduce data before it reaches the host
idea: Two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live in its arms; likewise CXL memory expanders carry local filter, aggregate, top-k and embedding-pooling engines so the host receives answers rather than raw rows, eliminating host-side staging buffers and duplicate working copies.
why: Host DRAM and data movement: 2-4x less host buffer memory for analytics and recommendation, 5-10x less link traffic.

title: Integrate-and-fire checkpoints store only threshold-crossing activations
idea: Saved activations for backprop are recorded like spikes: each neuron accumulates its value against a membrane threshold and only crossings are written as (index, quantized value) events; dense tensors are never materialized and are reconstructed from events plus a leak model during the backward pass.
why: Training activation memory: 4-10x fewer bytes for sparsely activated layers (ReLU-family, MoE).

title: Magnetosome-chain ordering aligns embedding rows for delta compression
idea: As magnetotactic bacteria align magnetosomes into a chain along the field, a one-time pass sorts embedding-table rows along a learned principal axis or space-filling curve so neighbors are similar, then stores each row as an entropy-coded delta from its predecessor; a small index maps original IDs to chain positions.
why: Recommendation embeddings occupy terabytes of DRAM; 2-4x compression decodable at line rate.

title: Seed dormancy with cue-triggered germination for cold pages
idea: Cold pages are dried into compact 'seeds' (compressed to ~25%) in a far tier; a tiny learned cue detector watches request streams for germination cues (user login, job phase markers, specific syscalls) and rehydrates exactly those seeds ahead of use, as seeds sprout on temperature and moisture cues rather than on demand.
why: Tiering: lets 40-60% of resident data leave DRAM with fewer demand-miss stalls than recency-based tiering.

title: Brood-to-honey comb reuse time-multiplexes training buffers
idea: Bee comb cells switch from rearing brood to storing honey; the compiler likewise assigns each physical DRAM region a planned succession of roles (forward activation, then gradient, then optimizer scratch) from a global lifetime graph with in-place kernels, so no region idles between roles.
why: Training peak memory: 25-40% lower peak footprint per accelerator.

title: Tardigrade vitrification swaps idle KV cache for token transcript
idea: When a chat session goes idle, its multi-GB KV cache is 'desiccated' to the token transcript plus a 1-2% anchor subset of KV states; on return the session is rehydrated by parallel prefill seeded from the anchors, like a tardigrade reviving from its tun state.
why: Inference capacity: idle sessions hold ~1000x less memory, so 5-10x more concurrent sessions per GB.

title: Kanerva sparse distributed memory replaces per-token KV slots
idea: Instead of one slot per token, keys are written into a fixed set of hard locations activated within a Hamming radius and values are superposed into counters there (Kanerva's cerebellum-inspired SDM); retrieval reads the activated locations, so memory grows with information content, not sequence length.
why: Long-context KV: a fixed 64 MB memory serving million-token contexts approximately.

title: Holographic binding bundles low-priority tokens into superposed vectors
idea: Peripheral KV pairs are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations, akin to distributed cortical traces) and summed into a few bundle vectors per block; queries unbind to recover approximate values, cleaned up against a small codebook.
why: KV capacity: 8-16x compression on the long tail of context.

title: Dendritic subarrays compute attention scores where the keys live
idea: Neurons integrate synaptic inputs on dendrites before the soma; DRAM subarrays likewise perform bit-serial dot products of a broadcast query against stored keys using charge-sharing logic beside the sense amplifiers, and only top-k indices leave the bank, so no staging copy of the KV cache is needed in HBM.
why: HBM capacity and data movement: removes duplicate KV staging and cuts attention read energy 5-10x.

title: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve erodes low-order bits of aging data
idea: Tagged tensors (cached activations, retrieval embeddings, KV) lose least-significant bits on a forgetting schedule unless re-accessed, with each access acting as rehearsal that resets the clock; the controller periodically repacks eroded lines into denser formats.
why: Capacity: 2-3x density for approximation-tolerant aging data, with loss concentrated on rarely used items.

title: Alternative splicing assembles many fine-tuned models from shared exons
idea: A library of weight blocks (exons) is stored once; each task variant is a splice map selecting and ordering blocks plus tiny per-variant tweaks, the way one gene yields many proteins, so serving 100 fine-tunes needs one exon library rather than 100 copies.
why: Model-zoo serving: 10-50x less DRAM than full copies, sharing at block granularity beyond adapter methods.

title: Overlapping reading frames share MSB bit-planes between correlated tensors
idea: Viruses read one RNA in shifted frames to make different proteins; a base model and its fine-tunes (or strongly correlated projections) store a shared most-significant bit-plane once, each variant keeping only its own low-order planes, read through frame-specific offsets.
why: Capacity: 30-50% savings for families of correlated weights.

title: Quorum sensing decides when shared pages get local replicas
idea: Bacteria act only when autoinducer concentration crosses a threshold; each host counts remote accesses to a pooled page from its cores, makes a local replica only when demand crosses a quorum, and dissolves it when the signal decays, otherwise serving the page from the shared CXL pool.
why: Replication overhead: 30-60% fewer duplicate copies of shared data in pooled racks.

title: Fly mushroom-body hashing finds near-duplicate pages for delta storage
idea: Fruit flies tag odors via random sparse expansion then winner-take-all; the controller applies the same FlyHash to sampled page contents to bucket near-duplicates, storing each as a delta against a bucket representative (checkpoints, VM snapshots, model replicas with slight drift).
why: Capacity: catches near-duplicates that exact-hash dedup misses, a further 1.3-2x.

title: Scatter-hoarding stashes intermediates in idle SRAM, recomputes lost ones
idea: Squirrels scatter caches widely and tolerate losing some; the runtime scatters short-lived activations across idle SRAM and register files of neighboring accelerators over the fabric, accepts eviction without notice, and recomputes lost items from cheap upstream checkpoints.
why: HBM capacity: 15-30% less DRAM for activations by harvesting stranded SRAM across a pod.

title: Apoptotic eat-me telemetry retires memory packages before they fail
idea: Like cells displaying phosphatidylserine before apoptosis, each DRAM package exports correctable-error rate, retention drift and hammer-count signals; crossing a threshold triggers live migration of its pages and schedules a tool-less swap of just that unit, so failures never crash jobs or force whole-board scrap.
why: Repairability: removes ~10% just-in-case DRAM headroom and extends module life 2-3x, cutting replacement demand.

title: Artificial-reef carriers house retired DDR4 DIMMs as CXL memory
idea: Coral reefs grow on sunken wrecks; a CXL Type-3 carrier card with standard DIMM slots and an inline compression engine lets operators move retired DDR4 RDIMMs into new servers as a compressed second tier, with tool-less DIMM swaps and the carrier itself reused across server generations.
why: Supply: returns decommissioned DDR4 to service; 30-50% less new DDR5 per server.

title: Salmon-run return: retired GPUs serve their HBM as KV pools
idea: Salmon die upstream and fertilize the forest; aging training GPUs are redeployed as dedicated KV-cache and expert-weight memory nodes over NVLink or RDMA, running only memory-serving firmware, so their HBM keeps supplying fast capacity to new accelerators instead of being shredded.
why: HBM supply: recovers 80+ GB of HBM per retired GPU, reducing new HBM needed for inference growth.

title: Salamander regeneration: rewritable row remapping that never runs out
idea: One-time fuse-based post-package repair is replaced by a rewritable on-module remap SRAM plus spare rows reserved per bank, so as cells weaken with age the module regrows healthy rows indefinitely and recycled chips are re-repaired at every life cycle.
why: Lifetime and reuse yield: second-life DRAM usable at 95%+ capacity instead of being binned out.

title: Decomposer line recovers known-good DRAM dies from e-waste
idea: Like fungi turning logs back into nutrients, a low-temperature depackaging and test line recovers known-good DRAM dies from scrapped phones, laptops and DIMMs and re-packages them on a passive organic interposer as heavily ECC-protected far-memory chiplets.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: domestic urban-mine bit supply with no front-end fab.

title: Datacenter spleen grades and recirculates aging memory modules
idea: The spleen filters old red blood cells and recycles their iron; a campus test station receives every pulled module, characterizes retention, hammer threshold and speed, and re-dispatches it to the tier it can still serve (hot, warm, approximate, scrap), feeding results back to procurement.
why: Supply: longer useful life for every purchased bit; 20-30% less new DRAM procured per year.

title: Bone remodeling rotates hot rows to equalize aging stress
idea: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts continuously rebuild stressed bone; the controller migrates hot pages across banks and ranks on a slow schedule so hammer exposure, BTI aging and thermal stress spread evenly, leaving each chip with uniform, predictable remaining life that makes reuse grading simple.
why: Longer first life and higher reuse yield; fewer modules scrapped early from localized wear.

title: Pea-pod DIMMs with socketed packages replaced one at a time
idea: Like peas pulled from a pod, DRAM packages sit in low-profile LGA micro-sockets on the module, so one failing package is swapped in minutes and firmware remaps its range, instead of scrapping a 64-128 GB DIMM for one bad chip.
why: Repair: cuts DIMM scrap by ~80%, shrinking replacement DRAM demand.

title: Imaginal-disc HBM lifts off via pressure contacts for next boards
idea: Insect imaginal discs survive metamorphosis into the adult; HBM stacks mount to the interposer through anisotropic conductive film or micro-spring pressure contacts instead of permanent microbumps, so stacks can be lifted off a dead or obsolete accelerator and placed on its successor.
why: HBM supply and TSV-yield tax: one stack serves 2-3 accelerator generations.

title: Lichen pairing turns retired servers into RDMA memory donors
idea: Lichen fuses a fungus and an alga into a new organism; a stripped retired server (old CPU, full DRAM) runs a tiny memory-server OS and lends its DRAM over RDMA as remote swap to new servers, its only job being memory.
why: Supply: retiring servers' DRAM gets a second 3-5-year life; 25-40% less new DRAM per new server.

title: Genome-like health ledger travels with every memory module
idea: Each module stores a tamper-evident lifetime record (hours, temperature, ECC events, hammer counts, repairs) in extended SPD, like DNA carrying heritable history, readable by any buyer or recycler to price and place the module in its next life; mandated in procurement standards.
why: Secondary-market liquidity: makes used DRAM trustworthy, raising reuse rates and lowering new-bit demand.

title: Age polyethism assigns leaky aged chips to error-tolerant data
idea: Older worker ants take on riskier foraging jobs; recycled modules with weaker retention tails host data that tolerate rare flips (low-priority KV, activations, recomputable caches) under light ECC, while young chips hold critical state.
why: Reuse yield: turns marginal chips into useful capacity, adding 10-20% second-life supply.

title: Mitochondrial fusion merges two half-good modules into one
idea: Damaged mitochondria fuse to complement each other's defects; the controller interleaves the healthy banks of two partially failed modules into one full-capacity logical rank via a per-bank map, so modules with dead banks are combined rather than scrapped.
why: Repair: recovers 5-15% more usable bits from fleet failures.

title: Grafted controller mezzanine upgrades compression without scrapping DRAM
idea: Gardeners graft new scions onto old rootstock; CXL memory modules put the DRAM on a long-lived rootstock board and the controller and compression ASIC on a pluggable mezzanine, so better compression or a new link standard is adopted by swapping a small card rather than the DRAM.
why: Capital and supply: each DRAM bit's effective capacity rises over its life (1.5x to 3x) and it outlives link generations.

title: Hermit-crab vacancy chains cascade memory through fleet tiers
idea: Hermit crabs line up by size and swap shells in a chain when a large new shell appears; a fleet protocol makes every new HBM or DDR5 purchase trigger a planned cascade (training, inference, CXL pool, edge, recycler) with standardized sleds and internal transfer prices at each step.
why: Supply strategy: average bit lifetime from ~4 to 8-10 years, roughly halving new-bit demand for equal capacity.

title: Starfish regrowth: compression slack pays for erasure-coded memory
idea: A starfish regrows from one arm; pages are compressed and the freed space holds erasure-code parity striped across modules, so any single module can be hot-pulled for repair and rebuilt from the rest with no net capacity cost.
why: Repair without downtime or overprovisioning; makes cheaper, less reliable recycled modules safe to deploy.

title: Hydra stem-cell spare pool differentiates into failed modules
idea: Hydra renews itself from stem cells; each rack keeps 3-5% of memory as undifferentiated hot spares that silently mirror compressed copies of the most failure-prone ranges and instantly take over an address range, with dead units swapped in monthly batch maintenance.
why: Replaces per-server 10-20% headroom with rack-level 3-5% while letting fleets run aged modules.

title: Liver-style compensatory compression covers modules out for repair
idea: The liver regrows mass to keep function after losing tissue; when modules are pulled for repair the memory manager raises compression levels on the remaining DRAM to hold logical capacity constant, then relaxes it after reinsertion, so maintenance never shrinks jobs.
why: Removes 5-10% maintenance headroom and makes hot repair routine.

title: Blind-spot filling-in regenerates lost weight blocks approximately
idea: The visual cortex fills the retina's blind spot from its surroundings; weights are stored with a tiny per-layer predictor so if a recycled chip's bank dies, its weight blocks are regenerated from neighboring blocks plus a stored residual sketch, keeping the model serving until the part is swapped.
why: Lets cheap recycled DRAM hold weights without full mirroring; ~2x less redundancy overhead.

title: Plasmid-style updatable row-hammer defenses extend old dense DRAM
idea: Bacteria swap plasmids to gain new resistances; the CXL or buffer controller carries an embedded FPGA region whose hammer-tracking logic is updated over the air as new access patterns emerge, so vulnerable modules are patched rather than replaced.
why: Row hammer (~1k activations): avoids premature retirement of dense modules and keeps the reuse market viable.

title: Universal genetic code standard for portable compressed pages
idea: Every organism reads the same genetic code; an open, versioned compressed-page format lets a page compressed on one vendor's module move bit-for-bit to another's during repair or recycling without decompression or vendor lock-in.
why: Keeps 2-3x effective capacity intact across hardware swaps and makes compression tiers repairable.

title: Pollinator robots move memory sleds to where demand blooms
idea: Bees ferry pollen between flowers; rack robots carry blind-mate, hot-plug CXL memory sleds rated for thousands of insertions from underused racks to those whose KV and batch demand will peak, guided by tomorrow's forecast.
why: Utilization: 20-30% less DRAM fleet-wide by moving bits to demand instead of provisioning every rack for its own peak.

title: Zebrafish-heart regeneration: spare die and reroutable TSVs in HBM
idea: Zebrafish regrow damaged heart muscle; each HBM stack carries one spare core die and redundant TSV lanes, and field logic bypasses a failing die and reroutes broken TSVs, so the stack is repaired in place instead of the whole accelerator being scrapped.
why: HBM TSV yield tax (20-30%) and field failures: fewer scrapped stacks and GPUs per usable GB.
